statement
Neither study can show that no responder has ever been poisoned: news reports are a selected record in which testing was almost never mentioned, and one incident gives no rate.

A later NIOSH article (Chiu et al., 2019: seven NIOSH authors, two of whom also wrote that report; no funding and no conflicts of interest declared; read as its author manuscript) summarizes two other incidents that NIOSH investigated, from 2017 and 2018, chosen to illustrate different scenarios; neither is the incident of that report. In the first, during a traffic stop, wind blew powder from a container onto an officer in short sleeves and without gloves, who cleaned hands and arms with hand sanitizer; within 5 minutes the officer felt disoriented and lightheaded, with blurry vision, and ambulance staff washed the skin with water and found the officer alert, with pupils of 4 mm, a breathing rate of 17 a minute and raised blood pressure and heart rate; no laboratory test was done, the officer was discharged with an assessment of chemical exposure, and the laboratory later found fentanyl with methamphetamine in the powder left in the container. In the second, four officers became lightheaded or dizzy, among other symptoms, after a call to a hotel room with drug powders in view: three who had entered the room, about 25 to 90 minutes after the response began, and one who never entered, 30 to 45 minutes after handling a camera and other items from the room that showed no visible contamination; one officer slumped to the ground and improved rapidly after a colleague gave naloxone; none was reported to have depressed breathing (one officer's breathing rate ranged from 9 to 20 a minute in the emergency department), all were alert with no documented constricted pupils, and their urine screens, which cannot detect fentanyl, were negative; the laboratory found fentanyl, a fentanyl analogue, heroin, cocaine, methamphetamine and cathinones in the room. Nothing was measured in the air, on surfaces or skin, or in blood, and perceived risk was not assessed. The authors judge that no officer's effects were consistent with severe opioid toxicity, consider breathing in, the lining of the eyes, nose or mouth, swallowing and the skin all possible routes, and read the one officer's improvement after naloxone as suggesting that opioids played a substantial part, an inference from one uncontrolled observation in an officer whose urine screen could not detect fentanyl; like NIOSH's report, they state that brief skin contact with fentanyl powder is not expected to be toxic when visible contamination is promptly removed, and they add that alcohol-based hand sanitizer may increase absorption. None of these studies can show that no responder has ever been poisoned: news reports are a selected record in which testing was almost never mentioned, and three incidents, investigated because officers fell ill, give no rate.

evidence_add.locator: Results › HHE 1, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (PDF p. 3, the 3rd continued on p. 4); Figure 1 legend (PDF p. 14); Table 2 and its footnotes (PDF p. 16)
evidence_add.extracted: HHE 1: during a traffic stop and vehicle search, a police officer in a short-sleeved uniform and without gloves opened an unlabelled rubber container outside the vehicle, and a gust of wind blew powder from it onto the officer, who reported powder all over the officer and the uniform; the officer brushed it off and cleaned hands and arms with hand sanitizer. Within 5 minutes the officer was disoriented and lightheaded, with blurry vision. The ambulance arrived about 10 minutes after onset; EMS staff washed the exposed skin with water and found the officer alert, with blood pressure 175/127 mmHg, breathing rate 17 a minute, heart rate 105 a minute and pupils of 4 mm, reactive; during transport the officer had intermittent trouble thinking and staying awake. At the emergency department, about 42 minutes after onset, the officer was alert with no constricted pupils; during transport and the visit the heart rate was 80–85, the breathing rate 15–21 and the blood pressure 149/77 to 159/104; mild blurry vision resolved after several hours; no laboratory tests were done; the discharge assessment was chemical exposure. The forensic laboratory identified fentanyl and methamphetamine in the powder left in the container (1.56 g), and fentanyl in a compressed tan powder (9.98 g); the Figure 1 legend says material in a paper wrapper beside the container contained fentanyl. Editors' notes: the one incident on file in which powder later found to contain fentanyl reached an officer's uncovered skin, as the account implies (short sleeves, no gloves, hands and arms cleaned, exposed skin washed); nothing was measured on the officer and no test was done; the powder also reached the uniform outdoors in wind, so breathing it in or contact with the eyes, nose or mouth are not excluded (the authors consider all routes possible, PDF p. 6); the powder also contained methamphetamine, and raised blood pressure and heart rate are among the effects of stimulants the authors list (PDF p. 5); constricted pupils or slowed breathing, signs of opioid toxicity, were not recorded.

evidence_add.locator: Results › HHE 2, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (PDF p. 4, the 3rd continued on p. 5); Table 1 (PDF p. 15); Table 2 (PDF p. 16)
evidence_add.extracted: HHE 2: four officers became ill during a response to a 911 call about an unconscious person with a possible overdose in a hotel room. Three entered, saw drug paraphernalia and powders scattered in plain view and heard the toilet flushed many times; they wore short sleeves, two wore gloves on entry and the third put gloves on shortly after, and they took turns to put on half-facepiece respirators with P-100 filters once powders were seen. One went back to headquarters to process a search warrant, using a computer and a camera used in the room; the fourth officer, who did not enter the room, helped there, handling the camera and other items from the room that had no visible contamination. Symptoms (lightheadedness or dizziness in all, with blurry vision, weakness, warmth, sweating, headache, numbness of both hands and the tongue, or feeling drunk, high or groggy) began about 25 to 90 minutes after the initial response for the three who entered, and about 30–45 minutes after first handling the equipment for the fourth (Table 1). One officer at the scene was helped out of the room, slumped against the wall and then to the ground, and improved rapidly after a colleague gave one dose of intranasal naloxone. After decontamination, none was reported to have depressed breathing; in the emergency department all were alert and oriented, none had documented constricted pupils, and the electrocardiograms were normal; blood pressure and heart rate were normal to raised, three had normal to raised breathing rates, and the fourth officer a rate ranging from 9 to 20 a minute; the officer given naloxone had no blood test, and the urine of all four was negative on a screen for cannabinoids, phencyclidine, cocaine, opiates, amphetamines, benzodiazepines and barbiturates; all were discharged after several hours. The emergency physicians' impressions were possible accidental overdose for the officer given naloxone and possible fentanyl exposure for the other three (Table 1). In the hotel room the laboratory identified dibutylone, N-ethylpentylone (2.87 g), heroin (0.14 g), para-fluoroisobutyryl fentanyl, cocaine, methamphetamine and fentanyl (0.14 g) (Table 2); the Results call these opioids, cocaine, methamphetamine and cathinones. Editors' notes: the opiate screen cannot detect fentanyl or its analogues, and most amphetamine screens do not readily detect synthetic cathinones (the article, PDF p. 7), so no officer had a test able to detect the fentanyl, the analogue or the cathinones found in the room; when the urine was collected is not reported; nothing was measured in the air, on surfaces or on the officers.

evidence_add.extracted: The authors judge that the five officers' health effects were not consistent with severe (life-threatening or late-stage) opioid toxicity, whose signs include profound lethargy, shallow, slow or absent breathing, constricted pupils, slow heart rate and low body temperature; they write that low-dose opioid exposure may give milder symptoms along a continuum, that non-specific symptoms such as nausea and lightheadedness reported by the officers fit it, and that the improvement after naloxone in one officer suggests that opioids were a substantial component of a mixed exposure; low-level mixtures with stimulants, and adulterants, might explain the variety of effects. Perceived risk, which can be linked to anxiety and symptom reporting apart from physical exposure, was not assessed. Breathing in, absorption through mucous membranes, swallowing and absorption through the skin were all possible routes in both incidents; brief skin contact with fentanyl powder, or powder of an analogue, is not expected to cause toxic effects if visible contamination is promptly removed (citing three sources, among them the ACMT and AACT statement); alcohol-based hand sanitizer, as used in HHE 1, may increase absorption of fentanyl powder. Negative urine screens do not rule out exposure: opiate screens will not detect synthetic opioids such as fentanyl, synthetic cathinones are not readily detected by most amphetamine screens, the amphetamine and cocaine screens were negative at cut-offs of 500 ng/mL and 150 ng/mL, and results under a cut-off are reported as negative. Stated limitations: retrospective evaluations, interviews weeks to months after the incidents, review of the acute emergency department records only, and toxicological data not always available. Editors' notes: nausea appears in no officer's reported symptoms in the Results or Table 1 (PDF pp. 3–4, 15); the reading of the naloxone response rests on one uncontrolled observation in an officer who had no blood test and whose urine screen could not detect fentanyl; nothing was measured on the officers or around them, so the article neither confirms nor excludes opioid poisoning in any officer.

evidence_add.extracted: An article by seven NIOSH authors (Chiu, Hornsby-Myers, de Perio, Snawder, Wiegand, Trout, Howard) summarizing two NIOSH Health Hazard Evaluations, requested by law enforcement agencies, of incidents in two states in 2017 and 2018 involving five officers: NIOSH staff visited each agency, interviewed the officers with health effects and others, and reviewed medical records, the agencies' documentation and forensic laboratory results for evidence samples, with body-camera footage in HHE 2 only. The two incidents were chosen to illustrate different scenarios that might lead to exposure and health effects; other NIOSH evaluations are pointed to on a web page. References 10 and 11 are the two evaluation reports: a New Hampshire report on one officer (HETA No. 2018-0132-3322, August 2018) and a Virginia report on officers (HETA No. 2018-0113-3325, September 2018), both by Chiu, Hornsby-Myers and Trout. No funding source for the work or the article; the authors declare no conflicts of interest; ethics review was not considered necessary (a public health activity), and written consent was obtained for the release of medical records. Read as the PubMed Central author manuscript, whose pages differ from the published article (Am J Ind Med 62(5):439–447). Editors' notes: neither incident is the one in NIOSH Health Hazard Evaluation Report No. 2018-0118-3331 (Jackson et al., 2018; anchors 12 to 15), which has another number and describes two officers, a locked metal box and no opioid identified, against one officer and a rubber container holding fentanyl (HHE 1) and four officers and a hotel room (HHE 2); this article does not cite it. Which incident happened in which year and state is not stated; the report titles suggest that HHE 1 is the New Hampshire evaluation. Two authors (Chiu, Hornsby-Myers) also wrote the 2018 report, so the two NIOSH sources are not independent.

evidence_set: Introduction, 3rd paragraph (p. 1, right column) and 4th paragraph (p. 2, left column); Discussion, 4th paragraph, Funding sources and Declarations of Interest (p. 5); reference list, entries DEA (2016) and Persaud & Jennings (2019) (p. 6)

Introduction: in 2016 the DEA released a 4-minute roll-call training video that, the authors write, wrongly warned officers that skin contact with fentanyl could be fatal, with testimonials from two officers who said they had had overdose symptoms after handling a fentanyl-related substance, and told viewers that an amount like a few grains of sand could kill; the DEA had removed it from its public website, but it was still on the US Department of Justice website in March 2021. A 2019 survey of New York first responders (cited as Persaud and Jennings, 2019) is reported as finding that nearly 80% believed that even briefly touching fentanyl could be deadly. Limitations: the sample was small and not random, officers were identified by agency contacts, the responses do not reflect law enforcement generally or even the agencies studied, and the agencies were chosen purposively. Funding: the overall study was supported by Arnold Ventures (grant 19-02661), while the same section says that the authors received no financial support for the research, authorship or publication of this article; no conflicts of interest reported. Editors' notes: the New York survey is now on file (Persaud and Jennings, 2020, card sc_persaud_2020, anchors 12 to 14): in an online pilot survey of February and March 2019, 149 of the 187 New York State responders analysed (79.7%) agreed with a statement that briefly touching fentanyl could be deadly (86 of 92 in law enforcement, 63 of 95 in fire or emergency medical services), in a self-selected sample with no knowable response rate. Nearly 80% is right, but believed is the citing authors' word for agreement at levels the survey does not report, and its statement says briefly, not even briefly. This paper dates the roll-call video to 2016 in its text (p. 1) and reference list (p. 6); Herman et al. (2020, anchor 15) give the same video, at the same Justice Department web address, as of 6 June 2017.

evidence_add.locator: Methods, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Results, 1st to 4th paragraphs; Table 1 (PDF p. 2); Limitations, 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 4)
evidence_add.extracted: An online pilot survey (SurveyMonkey), open from 1 February to 31 March 2019, written by the authors from a literature review and said to be validated for accuracy by experts in EMS, fire and law enforcement, with fifteen 6-point statements on risk perception (strongly disagree to strongly agree, with no middle option) and questions on knowledge and demographics. A flyer with the link and a QR code went to 15 associations of fire, police and emergency medical technicians in New York and nationally; 3 acknowledged and said they would distribute it; flyers were posted at the authors' universities, and first responders linked to those institutions shared it informally; agencies did not have to say whether they distributed it, so the overall study base cannot be ascertained. 247 responses were received; 187 came from responders serving New York State and no other state had more than 9, so only New York was analysed: law enforcement 92, EMS 55, fire and EMS dual role 25, fire 15 (Table 1). A majority of all disciplines had more than 15 years of experience, and 53.5% had encountered fentanyl or suspected fentanyl at work. Editors' notes: a self-selected convenience sample with no knowable response rate; the 60 responses from outside New York (247 − 187) are not described; 53.5% fits 100 of 187.

evidence_add.locator: Table 2, rows on briefly touching fentanyl and on breathing airborne fentanyl (PDF p. 3); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 4)
evidence_add.extracted: Table 2 reports each statement only as agree or disagree, by occupation. Briefly touching fentanyl could be deadly: fire, EMS or dual role, agree 63 (66.3%) and disagree 32 (33.7%) of 95; law enforcement, agree 86 (93.5%) and disagree 6 (6.5%) of 92. Breathing airborne fentanyl is dangerous to my health: agree 86 (90.5%) and 92 (100%). The Discussion gives 79.7% of responses agreeing that briefly touching fentanyl could be deadly, which the authors suggest miscommunication and misinformation may have caused, and states that research has shown brief contact is not deadly. Editors' calculations: 149 of 187 agreed (79.7%; Wilson 95% interval 73.3% to 84.8%) and 38 disagreed; law enforcement 27.2 percentage points higher (Newcombe interval about 16.0 to 37.7); the airborne statement 178 of 187 (95.2%). The paper does not say how the six answer levels were grouped into agree and disagree, so slight and strong agreement cannot be separated.

evidence_add.extracted: Information sources on fentanyl exposure and safety (all that apply): seminars or courses 78.1%, department training 76.5%, federal agencies 67.4%, professional or labor organizations 46.0%, social media or internet pages 23.0%, news media 13.9%; the authors read this as a sizable majority relying on official sources. The abstract and Conclusions say respondents generally agreed with expert risk perceptions, with lower agreement on hand sanitizer, glove type and skin exposure; the Conclusions add that the knowledge gaps reflect a need for better training through authoritative sources and a possible effect of overreliance on media reports of adverse effects from casual exposure. The Introduction says early warnings from law enforcement sources (reference 7, a DEA nationwide alert published in March 2015) may have heightened concerns, and that authoritative guidance rates the likelihood of an overdose from skin contact as very low (reference 8, a NIOSH video on preventing occupational exposure, published in March 2019; reference 9, the 2017 ACMT and AACT statement). The Discussion also states, citing reference 9, that harm from touching fentanyl is rather a chronic or long-term issue for people who touch it regularly or for long periods. Funding: none, apart from administrative support from the Christian Regenhard Center for Emergency Response Studies; no conflict-of-interest statement. Editors' notes: sources were asked about fentanyl in general and are not linked to any answer, so the survey cannot show where the belief came from, and the suggestion about media reports rests on no analysis (only 13.9% named news media); the 2017 statement contains no passage on chronic harm and says that no persistent effects are expected without prolonged lack of oxygen (Moss et al., 2017, PDF pp. 1, 4); the paper does not mention the DEA roll-call video.
